units.text: Process a binary file as if it were text; this is equivalent to the ‘⟦0⟧’ option.
units.sourceHTML: Process a binary file as if it were text; this is equivalent to the ‘--binary-files=text’ option.

units.text: If a file’s data or metadata indicate that the file contains binary data, assume that the file is of type ⟦0⟧. Non-text bytes indicate binary data; these are either output bytes that are improperly encoded for the current locale (see ⟦1⟧Environment Variables⟦2⟧), or null input bytes when the ⟦3⟧ (⟦4⟧) option is not given (see ⟦5⟧Other Options⟦6⟧).
units.sourceHTML: If a file’s data or metadata indicate that the file contains binary data, assume that the file is of type type. Non-text bytes indicate binary data; these are either output bytes that are improperly encoded for the current locale (see Environment Variables), or null input bytes when the -z (--null-data) option is not given (see Other Options).

units.text: By default, ⟦0⟧ is ‘⟦1⟧’, and ⟦2⟧ suppresses output after null input binary data is discovered, and suppresses output lines that contain improperly encoded data. When some output is suppressed, ⟦3⟧ follows any output with a message to standard error saying that a binary file matches.
units.sourceHTML: By default, type is ‘binary’, and grep suppresses output after null input binary data is discovered, and suppresses output lines that contain improperly encoded data. When some output is suppressed, grep follows any output with a message to standard error saying that a binary file matches.

units.text: If ⟦0⟧ is ‘⟦1⟧’, when ⟦2⟧ discovers null binary data in an input file it assumes that any unprocessed input does not match; this is equivalent to the ⟦3⟧ option. In this case the region of unprocessed input starts no later than the null binary data, and continues to end of file.
units.sourceHTML: If type is ‘without-match’, when grep discovers null binary data in an input file it assumes that any unprocessed input does not match; this is equivalent to the -I option. In this case the region of unprocessed input starts no later than the null binary data, and continues to end of file.

units.text: If ⟦0⟧ is ‘⟦1⟧’, ⟦2⟧ processes binary data as if it were text; this is equivalent to the ⟦3⟧ option.
units.sourceHTML: If type is ‘text’, grep processes binary data as if it were text; this is equivalent to the -a option.

units.text: When ⟦0⟧ is ‘⟦1⟧’, ⟦2⟧ may treat non-text bytes as line terminators even without the ⟦3⟧ (⟦4⟧) option. This means choosing ‘⟦5⟧’ versus ‘⟦6⟧’ can affect whether a pattern matches a file. For example, when ⟦7⟧ is ‘⟦8⟧’ the pattern ‘⟦9⟧’ might match ‘⟦10⟧’ immediately followed by a null byte, even though this is not matched when ⟦11⟧ is ‘⟦12⟧’. Conversely, when ⟦13⟧ is ‘⟦14⟧’ the pattern ‘⟦15⟧’ (period) might not match a null byte.
units.sourceHTML: When type is ‘binary’, grep may treat non-text bytes as line terminators even without the -z (--null-data) option. This means choosing ‘binary’ versus ‘text’ can affect whether a pattern matches a file. For example, when type is ‘binary’ the pattern ‘q$’ might match ‘q’ immediately followed by a null byte, even though this is not matched when type is ‘text’. Conversely, when type is ‘binary’ the pattern ‘.’ (period) might not match a null byte.

units.text: The heuristic that ⟦0⟧ uses to intuit whether input is binary is specific to ⟦1⟧ and may well be unsuitable for other applications, as it depends on command-line options, on locale, and on hardware and operating system characteristics such as system page size and input buffering. For example, if the input consists of a matching text line followed by nonmatching data that contains a null byte, ⟦2⟧ might either output the matching line or treat the file as binary, depending on whether the unprocessed input happens to include the matching text line.
units.sourceHTML: The heuristic that grep uses to intuit whether input is binary is specific to grep and may well be unsuitable for other applications, as it depends on command-line options, on locale, and on hardware and operating system characteristics such as system page size and input buffering. For example, if the input consists of a matching text line followed by nonmatching data that contains a null byte, grep might either output the matching line or treat the file as binary, depending on whether the unprocessed input happens to include the matching text line.

units.text: ⟦0⟧Warning:⟦1⟧ The ⟦2⟧ (⟦3⟧) option might output binary garbage, which can have nasty side effects if the output is a terminal and if the terminal driver interprets some of it as commands. On the other hand, when reading files whose text encodings are unknown, it can be helpful to use ⟦4⟧ or to set ‘⟦5⟧’ in the environment, in order to find more matches even if the matches are unsafe for direct display.
units.sourceHTML: Warning: The -a (--binary-files=text) option might output binary garbage, which can have nasty side effects if the output is a terminal and if the terminal driver interprets some of it as commands. On the other hand, when reading files whose text encodings are unknown, it can be helpful to use -a or to set ‘LC_ALL='C'’ in the environment, in order to find more matches even if the matches are unsafe for direct display.

units.text: If an input file is a device, FIFO, or socket, use ⟦0⟧ to process it. If ⟦1⟧ is ‘⟦2⟧’, all devices are read just as if they were ordinary files. If ⟦3⟧ is ‘⟦4⟧’, devices, FIFOs, and sockets are silently skipped. By default, devices are read if they are on the command line or if the ⟦5⟧ (⟦6⟧) option is used, and are skipped if they are encountered recursively and the ⟦7⟧ (⟦8⟧) option is used. This option has no effect on a file that is read via standard input.
units.sourceHTML: If an input file is a device, FIFO, or socket, use action to process it. If action is ‘read’, all devices are read just as if they were ordinary files. If action is ‘skip’, devices, FIFOs, and sockets are silently skipped. By default, devices are read if they are on the command line or if the -R (--dereference-recursive) option is used, and are skipped if they are encountered recursively and the -r (--recursive) option is used. This option has no effect on a file that is read via standard input.

units.text: If an input file is a directory, use ⟦0⟧ to process it. By default, ⟦1⟧ is ‘⟦2⟧’, which means that directories are read just as if they were ordinary files (some operating systems and file systems disallow this, and will cause ⟦3⟧ to print error messages for every directory or silently skip them). If ⟦4⟧ is ‘⟦5⟧’, directories are silently skipped. If ⟦6⟧ is ‘⟦7⟧’, ⟦8⟧ reads all files under each directory, recursively, following command-line symbolic links and skipping other symlinks; this is equivalent to the ⟦9⟧ option.
units.sourceHTML: If an input file is a directory, use action to process it. By default, action is ‘read’, which means that directories are read just as if they were ordinary files (some operating systems and file systems disallow this, and will cause grep to print error messages for every directory or silently skip them). If action is ‘skip’, directories are silently skipped. If action is ‘recurse’, grep reads all files under each directory, recursively, following command-line symbolic links and skipping other symlinks; this is equivalent to the -r option.

units.text: Skip any command-line file with a name suffix that matches the pattern ⟦0⟧, using wildcard matching; a name suffix is either the whole name, or a trailing part that starts with a non-slash character immediately after a slash (‘⟦1⟧’) in the name. When searching recursively, skip any subfile whose base name matches ⟦2⟧; the base name is the part after the last slash. A pattern can use ‘⟦3⟧’, ‘⟦4⟧’, and ‘⟦5⟧’…‘⟦6⟧’ as wildcards, and ⟦7⟧ to quote a wildcard or backslash character literally.
units.sourceHTML: Skip any command-line file with a name suffix that matches the pattern glob, using wildcard matching; a name suffix is either the whole name, or a trailing part that starts with a non-slash character immediately after a slash (‘/’) in the name. When searching recursively, skip any subfile whose base name matches glob; the base name is the part after the last slash. A pattern can use ‘*’, ‘?’, and ‘[’…‘]’ as wildcards, and \ to quote a wildcard or backslash character literally.

units.text: Skip files whose name matches any of the patterns read from ⟦0⟧ (using wildcard matching as described under ⟦1⟧).
units.sourceHTML: Skip files whose name matches any of the patterns read from file (using wildcard matching as described under --exclude).

units.text: Skip any command-line directory with a name suffix that matches the pattern ⟦0⟧. When searching recursively, skip any subdirectory whose base name matches ⟦1⟧. Ignore any redundant trailing slashes in ⟦2⟧.
units.sourceHTML: Skip any command-line directory with a name suffix that matches the pattern glob. When searching recursively, skip any subdirectory whose base name matches glob. Ignore any redundant trailing slashes in glob.

units.text: Process a binary file as if it did not contain matching data; this is equivalent to the ‘⟦0⟧’ option.
units.sourceHTML: Process a binary file as if it did not contain matching data; this is equivalent to the ‘--binary-files=without-match’ option.

units.text: Search only files whose name matches ⟦0⟧, using wildcard matching as described under ⟦1⟧. If contradictory ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ options are given, the last matching one wins. If no ⟦4⟧ or ⟦5⟧ options match, a file is included unless the first such option is ⟦6⟧.
units.sourceHTML: Search only files whose name matches glob, using wildcard matching as described under --exclude. If contradictory --include and --exclude options are given, the last matching one wins. If no --include or --exclude options match, a file is included unless the first such option is --include.

units.text: For each directory operand, read and process all files in that directory, recursively. Follow symbolic links on the command line, but skip symlinks that are encountered recursively. Note that if no file operand is given, grep searches the working directory. This is the same as the ‘⟦0⟧’ option.
units.sourceHTML: For each directory operand, read and process all files in that directory, recursively. Follow symbolic links on the command line, but skip symlinks that are encountered recursively. Note that if no file operand is given, grep searches the working directory. This is the same as the ‘--directories=recurse’ option.

units.text: For each directory operand, read and process all files in that directory, recursively, following all symbolic links.
units.sourceHTML: For each directory operand, read and process all files in that directory, recursively, following all symbolic links.
